li.a: American Mafia History: Greg Scarpa, Sr., "the Grim Reaper" and 30 Year FBI Informant
The Mob Museum: Did Gregory Scarpa Sr. mastermind the attempted assassination of Joe Colombo?
Gangsters Inc.: Profile of Colombo crime family capo Gregory "The Grim Reaper" Scarpa
Philadelphia Inquirer: N.Y. mob implodes; retired FBI agent cleared
CBS News: The FBI's Lin DeVecchio and "The Grim Reaper"
CBS News: Judge: FBI Made "Deal With The Devil"
NPR: FBI Agent on Trial Allegedly Aided Mob
All That's Interesting: Greg Scarpa, The Mafia Hitman Known As The 'Grim Reaper'
NBC News: Witness: FBI used mob muscle to crack '64 case

content.p: Gregory Scarpa Sr. was a captain in New York's Colombo crime family who spent decades as a secret source for the government agency that was investigating organised crime. Arrested for armed robbery in March 1962, he accepted a deal with the FBI and became a secret informant, a relationship that one history of his career puts at thirty years. He kept killing throughout. Estimates of his victims range from at least 12 during his years as an informant, according to CBS News, to at least 50, according to the Mob Museum.

His case became a test of how far the Bureau would go to keep a source. When his handler, agent Lindley DeVecchio, was tried for murder in 2007 over alleged leaks to Scarpa, the judge who ended the trial said the FBI had been willing to "make a deal with the devil". DeVecchio was never convicted: the prosecution collapsed and the charges were dismissed. Scarpa himself pleaded guilty to three murders in 1993 and died in a federal prison hospital the next year.

Scarpa was born on 8 May 1928, according to American Mafia History near Venice, Italy; other accounts say he was born to Italian immigrants and raised in Bensonhurst, Brooklyn. All That's Interesting reports that as a boy he helped his father deliver coal during the Depression. In the 1950s his brother Salvatore introduced him to the Colombo family. He married and had four children, and he also kept a long relationship with Linda Schiro, with whom he had two more.

He moved through gambling, loansharking, extortion, hijacking and murder, and he dressed well and carried large amounts of cash for bribes. He owned homes in Brooklyn, Manhattan, Florida and Las Vegas. He was the proprietor of the Wimpy Boys Social Club, a popular Mafia hangout, according to All That's Interesting. Schiro later said he sometimes left the numbers 666 on the pagers of important victims. His lawyer Louis Diamond called him "a true Machiavelli" who "lived to manipulate people against people", a remark quoted by All That's Interesting from a 1996 New Yorker piece.

After the March 1962 robbery arrest, the FBI offered Scarpa a way out. He had a lot to lose from a long sentence and, according to All That's Interesting, "hated doing time". He agreed to supply information. Gangsters Inc. says he soon grew into what the Bureau called a top echelon informant and quickly began using the FBI more than the FBI used him. His reputation helped. Other gangsters could hardly imagine that such a violent man was a rat.

The best-known story from this period concerns Mississippi. In the summer of 1964 three civil rights workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, vanished near Philadelphia, Mississippi, and were later found to have been killed by Klansmen. Linda Schiro told a Brooklyn court in 2007 that the FBI recruited Scarpa, flew him south, and handed him a gun in a hotel room, and that he put the gun in a Klansman's mouth to learn where the bodies lay. NBC News reported that the FBI has never acknowledged that Scarpa was involved. The Daily News reported in 1994, citing unnamed federal officials, that a frustrated J. Edgar Hoover had turned to Scarpa. American Mafia History adds a rival account from the journalist Jerry Mitchell, who claimed that a Mississippi highway patrolman named Maynard King got the grave locations from an anonymous tipster.

The Mob Museum says that FBI records do confirm the Mississippi story, and that Scarpa went back in 1966 to help find those responsible for the firebombing death of a civil rights leader. CBS News says he had a falling out with the Bureau and broke off relations, and American Mafia History dates his being dropped as an informant to January 1966.

CBS News says that in 1980 DeVecchio drove up to Scarpa's home unannounced and blocked his car in the driveway. "I want to get schooled in the life," DeVecchio remembered saying. About two weeks later Scarpa called and told him to come alone. Agents are not supposed to meet informants alone, but DeVecchio got special permission. (Schiro dated DeVecchio's arrival as handler to 1978; the other accounts say 1980.)

CBS reports that Scarpa's information helped the government's 1985 "Commission Case", which sent the heads of three of the five crime families away, and that Scarpa was paid $66,000 over 12 years. When Scarpa was arrested in 1985 for a credit card scam and pleaded guilty, American Mafia History says DeVecchio sent the judge a memo listing Scarpa's help to the FBI. Scarpa received five years of probation and a $10,000 fine, and some Colombo soldiers were surprised and wondered about his government ties.

DeVecchio told CBS that the two became friends. "I liked the guy," he said. "Doesn't mean I condone what he did." He also acknowledged getting close to the line. Asked by Anderson Cooper whether he had tipped Scarpa off before his son's expected arrest, DeVecchio said he had not. Asked if it was true that he had given Scarpa a pass, he said, "No, I don't think it's the truth at all."

In 1991 the Colombo family split between loyalists of the imprisoned boss Carmine Persico and the faction of acting boss Victor Orena. Scarpa sided with Persico. On 18 November 1991, according to Gangsters Inc., masked men fired at him as he left his home; nobody was hurt. American Mafia History says he drove off before shots were fired. Either way, he hunted Orena supporters in the following months.

The two sources differ on the details. Gangsters Inc. says he shot Vincent Fusaro dead as Fusaro hung Christmas lights in December 1991, and that in January 1992 he and Larry Mazza killed Nicholas Grancio. American Mafia History names Rosario Nastasa, Fusaro and James Malpiso as the dead and says Malpiso was hanging lights. Gangsters Inc. counts four killed and two wounded by Scarpa during the war.
CBS records that DeVecchio kept meeting him throughout the war. "He wasn't the only one conducting the war," DeVecchio told Cooper. "Everybody was shooting everybody."

In 1986 bleeding ulcers meant Scarpa needed transfusions, and he insisted on blood from people he knew. Gangsters Inc. says a crew member who injected steroids was infected with HIV and passed it on through his donation; All That's Interesting names him as Paul Mele. Scarpa kept the diagnosis secret.

In 1992 he was arrested on state firearms charges and indicted on federal racketeering charges involving three murders and put under house arrest. On 29 December 1992, American Mafia History says, he left his bed to confront two Lucchese family men who had threatened his stepson over a drug deal. In the gunfight he was shot in the eye. Prosecutors revoked the house arrest.

On 6 May 1993 he pleaded guilty to three murders and conspiracy to commit murder. He was sentenced to life on 15 December 1993, but that was cut to ten years because of his health, according to American Mafia History. He died on 4 June 1994. Early that year, the Mob Museum says, he told a fellow inmate, Alan Taglianetti, that his FBI status was about to become public, and insisted he "wasn't a rat". That inmate's later book claims Scarpa confessed a role in the 1971 shooting of Joe Colombo; the Mob Museum calls that link circumstantial. The Mob Museum says the news of his FBI work came out the following year.

CBS reports that prosecutors grew suspicious when Scarpa's son went on the run just before an arrest, and that members of Scarpa's crew who began cooperating said he had a source in law enforcement. Four FBI agents accused DeVecchio of leaking information. A Justice Department internal investigation found no basis to prosecute. DeVecchio retired in 1996.

In March 2006 the Brooklyn district attorney's office announced an indictment on four murder counts, alleging that DeVecchio had passed Scarpa information in return for cash, jewelry, liquor and prostitutes, between 1987 and 1992. He faced life in prison if convicted. The case depended mainly on Schiro. NPR reported Jerry Capeci's account that she had been paid $2,000 a month by the district attorney's office; she told the jury $2,200. She said DeVecchio visited weekly and took envelopes of cash. The defense called her an opportunist angling for a book deal. She admitted discussing book deals that would be "partly on truth and partly on fiction".

In the third week of trial, reporter Tom Robbins produced tapes from 1997 interviews with Capeci in which Schiro gave different accounts of three of the four killings. Prosecutor Michael Vecchione said that "had we been provided these tapes much earlier in the process, I daresay we wouldn't have been here." On 1 November 2007 the charges were dismissed. District Attorney Charles Hynes said the office would not have prosecuted had it heard the tapes. DeVecchio said, "This nightmare is over." Schiro's lawyer said she had told the truth in court.
Justice Gustin Reichbach also criticised the FBI. He said that "at best, the FBI engaged in a policy of self-deception, not wanting to know the true facts about this informant-murderer".
